acts.title: A bad first meeting
text: I met my wife’s parents for the first time in a restaurant, and for about four minutes it went well.
We managed the usual ___ — the journey, the weather, how quiet the street was.
Then her father asked me a question and I ___ him halfway through his own answer.
There was one of those ___ silences afterwards. Nobody looked at anybody.
Ten minutes later I ___ properly by asking what the flat had cost.
Her mother was clearly ___, although she was far too polite to say so.
We did not ___ that evening. It took about two years.

items.q: Stand too close and you might make somebody feel ___.
Getting these things wrong can lead to ___ or even cause offence.
It is easy to ___ your foot in it when you do not know the rules.
The “come here” sign is made by ___ your finger towards you.
A British person would not feel at ___ with a question about their salary.
Safer ___ of conversation include sport and the weather.
Voice ___ also differs greatly between cultures.
In some East Asian countries, silence is seen as ___ — it shows respect.

tts: Communication between people from different cultures involves far more than simply understanding each other’s words.

For communication to be successful, we need to be aware of other people’s rules of conversation — how far apart we should stand, which topics are acceptable, or whether it is all right to interrupt somebody or to be silent.
Getting these things wrong can lead to misunderstandings, or even cause offence.

So let us look first at personal space. In North America the average distance between two people who are not close friends is forty-five centimetres. In Western Europe it is a little less — thirty-six to forty. In Japan a respectful distance is around ninety centimetres, whereas in the Middle East twenty to thirty centimetres is the norm.
Stand too close and you might make somebody feel awkward; too far away and you give the impression of being distant and unfriendly.

items.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: The unspoken rules that differ from culture to culture
How to learn a foreign language faster
Why English became a global language

items.q: What does the speaker say successful communication needs?
o: Awareness of other people’s rules of conversation

items.q: Which distance does the speaker give for the Middle East?

tts: Another important aspect of cross-cultural communication is the number of silences in a conversation.
Most Europeans and North Americans avoid long silences. For them, silence suggests something negative — that you feel uncomfortable, or shy, or angry, or that you are not interested in the topic.
But in some East Asian countries silences are perfectly acceptable. In fact silence is seen as a positive thing. It shows respect; it shows you are listening.

Voice volume also differs greatly. People from South America, or southern Europe, tend to speak more loudly than people from northern Europe. It is easy to think a group of people from Brazil are having an argument when in fact they are just having an enthusiastic discussion.

Another key is knowing which topics are appropriate. In many countries, like China, it is very normal to ask somebody how old they are or how much they earn. But a person from the UK would not feel at ease with these questions.

And finally, gestures. The “come here” sign, made by curling your finger towards you, is extremely rude in many countries, including Slovakia and much of South East Asia. In the Philippines you can actually be arrested for making it.

items.s: Most North Americans are comfortable with long silences.
In some East Asian countries silence is understood as a sign of respect.
People from northern Europe generally speak more loudly than South Americans.
The speaker says a British person would be uncomfortable being asked about their salary.
The “come here” finger gesture means the same thing everywhere.

tts: How far apart do you stand during conversation?
Which topics are acceptable to talk about?
What makes somebody feel awkward in a conversation?
Who decides which topics are appropriate?
Could you tell me how far apart people stand?

items.q: “How far apart do you stand?” — where is the subject?
o: After the auxiliary: do YOU stand
items.why: An ordinary object question: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb.

items.q: “What makes somebody feel awkward?” — why is there no auxiliary?
o: Because the question word is the subject
items.why: When what or who IS the subject, no auxiliary appears and the word order does not change.

items.q: “Which topics are acceptable?” — what kind of question is this?
Which of these is the indirect version?
o: Could you tell me how far apart people stand?
How far apart do people stand?
items.why: An indirect question opens with a polite phrase and then uses statement word order.

acts.title: Three kinds of question
rule: English builds questions in three different shapes, and B2 is where the difference starts to matter. Which shape you need depends on one thing: what the question word is doing in the sentence.
points: The question word is the object. Question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. Who did you meet?
The question word IS the subject. No auxiliary at all, and statement order stays. Who met you?
Open with a polite phrase, then switch to statement order. No auxiliary inside the clause.
eg: Who taught you to whistle?
Subject question — who is doing the teaching, so no did.
Who did you teach?
Object question — who is the person taught, so did returns.
What happened at the meeting?
Subject question. Never “What did happen”.
What did they decide at the meeting?
Object question.
How many people speak Silbo?
Subject question — how many people is the subject.
How many languages do they speak?
Object question — how many languages is the object.
Could you tell me where the station is?
Indirect: statement order. Not “where is the station”.
Do you happen to know whether it opens on Sunday?
Indirect yes/no question: use whether or if.
I was wondering if you could help me.
Indirect and softer still. It is a statement, so it ends with a full stop.
What made you apply?
Subject question with make — very common, and almost always got wrong.
acts.careful: An indirect question is not a question in its word order. “Could you tell me where is the station?” is the commonest B2 error in this area.

steps.cue: Make it indirect with COULD YOU TELL ME
steps.a: Could you tell me where she works
steps.why: Statement order: where she works, not where does she work.

steps.cue: Make it softer still with I WAS WONDERING
steps.a: I was wondering where she works

items.from: Does the office open on Saturday?

steps.cue: Make it indirect with DO YOU KNOW
steps.a: Do you know whether the office opens on Saturday
alt: Do you know if the office opens on Saturday
steps.why: A yes/no question needs whether or if to join the two halves.

steps.cue: Make it more tentative with DO YOU HAPPEN TO KNOW
steps.a: Do you happen to know whether the office opens on Saturday
alt: Do you happen to know if the office opens on Saturday

items.from: Somebody taught her the gesture. You want to know who.

steps.cue: Ask it directly, as a SUBJECT question
Now ask it indirectly with COULD YOU TELL ME
steps.a: Could you tell me who taught her the gesture

steps.cue: Rewrite it with MADE and FEEL
Now make it indirect with I WONDER
steps.a: I wonder what made him feel upset

use: Do you happen to know whether…?

write.q: You are going to spend three months working in a country you have never visited. Write eight questions you would send to a colleague who lives there, about the unwritten rules of conversation. Include at least two subject questions, two indirect wh-questions and two indirect yes/no questions.
write.model:
1. Could you tell me how close people normally stand when they are talking?
2. What made you change the way you greet people after you moved there?
3. Do you happen to know whether it is rude to ask somebody what they do for a living?
4. Who decides these things — is it generational, or the same for everybody?
5. I was wondering if silence in a meeting means something different there.
6. What happens if you interrupt somebody more senior than you?
7. Do you know whether the “thumbs up” gesture is safe to use?
8. I was wondering if you could tell me the one mistake foreigners always make.
